name: Luminance Contrast Prediction Error and Aesthetic Response

mechanism_chain.description: Luminance contrast drives feedforward magnocellular signals to V1/V2. V1/V2 neurons compare feedforward luminance input against top-down predictions about expected luminance distribution given spatial context (Muckli & Petro, 2013). Luminance PE is the residual between actual and predicted luminance.

data.finding: V1/V2 neurons compare feedforward luminance input against top-down contextual predictions via non-geniculate feedback
data.effect: V1 activity modulated by spatial context predictions
data.design: Review of fMRI contextual modulation studies

data.finding: Luminance contrast drives magnocellular feedforward signals; mismatch with predicted luminance generates PE
data.effect: Luminance PE = residual between actual and predicted luminance
data.design: Computational model validated against V1 physiology

justification.backing: Luminance contrast drives feedforward magnocellular signals whose mismatch with contextual predictions generates PE in V1/V2. This is the same predictive processing mechanism as T1 but applied specifically to the luminance dimension. Muckli's work confirms that V1 actively predicts expected luminance given spatial context.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.70 reflects strong mechanistic evidence for luminance PE in V1. The mechanism operates at the earliest cortical processing stages and is well-supported by both computational models and neuroimaging.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) architectural luminance contrast is primarily processed through retinal adaptation mechanisms rather than cortical PE computation — simple light/dark adaptation would explain contrast responses without invoking prediction; (b) V1 luminance PE is negligible compared to other contrast computation mechanisms (e.g., retinal ganglion cell center-surround).

mechanism_chain.description: Moderate luminance PE (global contrast ratio 1:5–1:15, architecturally coherent shadow structure) generates resolvable prediction challenge → positive valence. Strother (2019): peak preference ratings at global contrast ratio 1:7–1:15 in architectural photographs. Effect size d ≈ 0.50 for preferred vs. flat-lighting conditions.

data.finding: Peak aesthetic preference for architectural scenes at global luminance contrast ratio 1:7 to 1:15
data.paradigm: Preference ratings for architectural photographs with manipulated global contrast
data.effect: Peak preference at 1:7-1:15 global contrast ratio

data.finding: Adequate luminance variation reveals spatial structure; insufficient or excessive contrast degrades spatial perception
data.effect: Preferred luminance range 50-300 cd/m² for work environments

justification.backing: Strother's systematic manipulation of global contrast in architectural photographs establishes the dose-response function. Peak preference at 1:7-1:15 corresponds to shadows that reveal spatial structure without overwhelming adaptation. Muckli (panel debate) added that these boundaries depend on SPATIAL STRUCTURE: architecturally coherent contrast (shadows on recognizable elements) produces more positive response than arbitrary patches at the same ratio.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.60 with EMPIRICAL_COVARIANCE warrant reflects that Strother's data are architectural-specific but not yet published in full parametric form. The boundary values are expert-calibrated from preliminary data. The confidence applies to architecturally coherent contrast distribution; incoherent contrast (arbitrary patches) produces lower preference at the same ratio.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) luminance contrast preference is dominated by semantic content (what the shadows reveal) rather than contrast magnitude per se; (b) the 1:7-1:15 range is specific to Strother's stimulus set and does not generalize to the diversity of real architectural lighting conditions.

mechanism_chain.description: High luminance PE (global contrast > 1:30) in specific spatial configuration (bright zone <20% of visual field surrounded by dark context — Plummer's shaft, chiaroscuro) generates categorical PE: light becomes visible AS A SUBSTANCE rather than surface illumination. Dual-adaptation state in V1 drives AX3 pathway activation.

data.finding: High luminance contrast (>1:30) in specific spatial configuration triggers awe-related physiological responses
data.paradigm: Architectural analysis of light-shaft configurations in sacred architecture
data.effect: Shaft of light (bright <20% visual field in dark surround) produces reported awe
data.design: Architectural case analysis with phenomenological description

data.finding: V1 processes extreme contrast through dual-adaptation state — separate adaptation to bright and dark regions
data.effect: Light becomes visible AS A SUBSTANCE when contrast exceeds adaptation range
data.design: Mechanistic proposal based on V1 adaptation physiology

justification.backing: The awe-trigger configuration (Plummer's shaft, chiaroscuro) requires specific spatial parameters: bright zone occupying less than 20% of visual field surrounded by substantially darker context. The dual-adaptation mechanism (Muckli) explains why this produces a qualitatively different perceptual experience: the visual system cannot adapt simultaneously to both regions, generating categorical PE where light is perceived as substance rather than surface illumination.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.55 with MECHANISM warrant reflects a well-motivated mechanistic account but limited direct empirical measurement of the awe response. The 20% fraction and 1:30 contrast threshold are expert estimates (Strother + Muckli, panel consensus) requiring psychophysical validation.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) the awe response to dramatic light is mediated by semantic/cultural associations (sacred space = awe) rather than by contrast-driven perceptual mechanisms — in which case the effect would be culturally specific, not universal; (b) the 1:30 threshold is too stimulus-specific to be architecturally useful as a design parameter.

mechanism_chain.description: Luminance exceeding retinal adaptation tolerance (point source > 2,000 cd/m²; DGP > 0.35) triggers discomfort via sustained accommodation effort, pupillary strain, and cortical arousal. Wienold & Christoffersen (2006): DGP > 0.35 produces 50% occupant dissatisfaction.

data.finding: Daylight Glare Probability >0.35 produces 50% occupant dissatisfaction
Point source luminance >2000 cd/m² produces disability glare via sustained accommodation effort and pupillary strain
data.effect: Disability glare threshold at ~2000 cd/m² for point source

justification.backing: Glare discomfort is the most well-established dose-response relationship in architectural lighting science. The DGP metric integrates luminance distribution, solid angle, and position index into a single probability of dissatisfaction. The 0.35 threshold is derived from extensive field measurements in occupied buildings.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.80 reflects the strongest empirical base in this template — glare research has decades of field validation with large samples. The DGP metric is standardized and widely used in building design. Population modifiers (migraine, elderly) shift the threshold but the basic relationship is robust.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) DGP is an inadequate metric for immersive architectural experience — some dramatic lighting that exceeds DGP 0.35 may be aesthetically valued (e.g., direct sun in a cathedral) despite producing measurable glare; (b) occupant adaptation and control can override the DGP-predicted dissatisfaction (people who choose to sit in sun accept higher glare).

noradrenergic_response.unit: ratio max:min luminance in visual field (cd/m²)
noradrenergic_response.flag: THEORETICAL_DEFAULT for exact boundaries — Strother data not yet published in full parametric form; boundaries expert-calibrated

awe_experience.notes: Shaft, chiaroscuro, aureole configurations meet this criterion. The 20% fraction is an expert estimate requiring direct psychophysical validation.

sense_of_coherence.description: Contrast on architecturally meaningful structures (coherent shadows) produces more positive aesthetic response than equivalent contrast from arbitrary sources.
sense_of_coherence.magnitude: +0.20 to +0.35 preference advantage for coherent vs. incoherent contrast at matched ratio

age_group.modifier: Preferred range shifts to 30–200 cd/m²; DGP threshold −0.05

interaction_templates.nature: Dappled light has 1/f luminance statistics — intersection of T1 and L1. Both activate simultaneously; joint activation is additive.
L1's high-PE awe-trigger configuration (contrast > 1:30, bright zone <20%) is the luminance-specific input to AX3. L1 is upstream; AX3 is downstream.
L1 is a partial confound in SC1 studies (high-integration spaces receive more daylight → luminance contrast). Article Eater should apply L1 partial-out when analyzing SC1 claims.

panel_reasoning_excerpt:
### Window Science and Daylighting

**5. Christoph Reinhart** (MIT, Building Technology Program)
Expert on daylight modeling and building simulation whose work quantifies the non-visual benefits of windows — not just illumination but view quality, daylight autonomy, and spatial daylight distribution (Reinhart et al., 2006, ~600 citations). His research demonstrates that window design involves a multi-objective optimization: maximizing daylight (L2/L3), managing glare (L1), providing view (this template), and controlling solar heat gain. The view function is often sacrificed to the other objectives — frosted glass for privacy, electrochromic glass for glare control, deep floor plates that push workstations away from windows.
*Role*: Provides the building-science perspective on window design as a view delivery system. Reinhart's work establishes that VIEW is a quantifiable window function — "view out" metrics (EN 17037) assess the quality of what is visible, including the fraction of sky, landscape, and ground visible from each workstation. This connects the psychological literature (Ulrich, Kaplan) to the architectural design process: view quality can be modeled, optimized, and specified.

**6. Lisa Heschong** (formerly Heschong Mahone Group; author of *Thermal Delight in Architecture*)
Researcher who conducted the landmark studies on daylight and human performance, demonstrating that students in classrooms with more daylight performed better on standardized tests, and that retail stores with skylights had higher sales (Heschong et al., 2002, ~500 citations). Her work separates the VIEW effect from the DAYLIGHT effect: students in rooms with windows to nature performed better than students in rooms with windows to built environments, even controlling for light levels. This suggests that view content contributes independently of illumination.
*Role*: Provides the evidence that separates view from daylight. Heschong's finding that view CONTENT matters (nature > built, controlling for light level) is critical for isolating the view mechanism from the daylight mechanism. In the PE framework: L2 and L3 formalize the light benefits of windows; VIEW-I formalizes the content benefits. Both operate through windows, but through different channels.

cross_template_interactions.IC2_body_budget: L1's glare extreme (DGP > 0.45) imposes sustained visual discomfort contributing to allostatic cost. Moderate contrast (Goldilocks zone) contributes to IC2 equilibrium. Chronic under-contrasted environments (uniform fluorescent lighting) deny the restorative visual prediction engagement that moderate PE provides.
cross_template_interactions.AX4_perceived_control: Occupant control over shading (operable blinds, electrochromic glazing) is a direct AX4 interaction. Glare from uncontrollable sources scores among the highest AX4 violations in post-occupancy surveys.

luminance_level.description: Uncontrolled direct sun creates extreme contrast (DGP > 0.50). External shading: −40–60% peak luminance.

material_surface_properties.description: High-reflectance walls within 3m of window reduce global contrast ratio by ~30–50%.

spatial_enclosure_ratio.description: ρ > 0.80 vs. ρ < 0.30: 25–40% reduction in contrast ratio.
